analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal labor law so workers can unionize, strike, and sue employers who retaliate.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in committee and its subcommittees until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act to make it much easier for workers to form unions and bargain collectively. It would expand who counts as a covered employee, ban permanently replacing striking workers, add fines of up to $50,000–$100,000 per violation for employers who break labor law, let workers sue employers directly in court, and force first contract negotiations through binding arbitration if bargaining stalls. It would also require federal contractors over $500,000 to disclose labor law violations and let employers and unions agree that all workers in a bargaining unit pay union fees, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize. The bill's own findings cite Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing union members earn about 25.6% more than nonunion workers, are 28% more likely to have job-based health insurance, and nearly 5 times more likely to have a defined-benefit pension [S3]. It would protect workers fired for union activity by adding real penalties and a private right to sue [S2][S3], and require federal contractors to disclose labor violations before winning contracts [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers seeking to organize and bargain

how_it_helps.text: Adds civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation — doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders — against employers who fire or retaliate against workers exercising labor rights, remedies the bill says are currently absent from the National Labor Relations Act [S2][S3].

Lets workers sue employers directly in federal court for labor violations, with back pay, front pay, consequential damages, and twice that amount in liquidated damages; today workers must rely on the National Labor Relations Board to prosecute their case and have no remedy if it declines [S3].
Bans employers from permanently replacing striking workers and makes discriminating against strikers an unfair labor practice [S2][S3].

If bargaining for a first contract stalls, a Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service process culminating in a binding arbitration panel would settle terms for two years, aimed at the problem the bill cites of roughly half of new organizing campaigns failing to reach a first agreement [S3].

Requires employers to post notices of workers' rights, gives unions voter lists of eligible employees after an election is scheduled, and narrows the definition of 'supervisor' so fewer workers can be classified out of labor law protections [S2][S3].

Requires federal contractors seeking contracts over $500,000 to disclose labor law violations from the prior three years, and bans federal contract money from being spent on campaigns persuading workers for or against unionizing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face new fines, court suits, and liquidated damages; companies that currently classify workers as independent contractors or supervisors to avoid union rules; and workers in right-to-work states, who could be required to pay union fees when unions and employers agree to fair-share provisions [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers violating labor law, and nonunion workers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on employers, including posting and notice obligations, penalties up to $100,000 per violation, personal liability for directors and officers, and mandatory arbitration of first contracts — provisions business groups argued raise costs and tilt the bargaining process heavily toward unions; no such industry objection appears in the provided sources, so this is the standard structural objection.
The fair-share provision would override state right-to-work laws, meaning workers who choose not to join the union could still be required to pay fees to it as a condition of employment [S3].

Directing the National Labor Relations Board to certify a union and issue a bargaining order without a rerun election when it finds the employer interfered — based on signed authorization cards — would shift a decision currently made by secret-ballot election to card-based certification [S3].
Making Board orders self-enforcing and immediately effective, with civil penalties for noncompliance, reduces the court review employers currently have before an order takes effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want to organize, the bill addresses real gaps: employer retaliation currently carries little penalty, workers cannot sue on their own, and about half of first contract negotiations fail. The costs are concentrated on employers and companies whose business model depends on classifying workers outside the law, plus a genuine trade-off for workers in right-to-work states who could be compelled to pay fees. The design is aggressive — card-based certification and binding arbitration of first contracts shift power decisively toward unions — but the core remedies close enforcement holes that other labor laws do not have.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which later referred pieces of it to subcommittees; neither committee ever took action, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the bill on June 13, 2018, with 34 original cosponsors, and 79 House Democrats cosponsored it in total; no Republicans did [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On October 19, 2018, it was referred to the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee and the Workforce Protections Subcommittee, where it sat [S5].
No markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business interests benefited, since the status quo — weak penalties, no private right of action, permanent replacement of strikers — stayed in place; the bill reappeared in the next Congress as the PRO Act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers opposing stronger labor law enforcement

industries.industry: Private-sector employers (large and mid-sized firms subject to the NLRA)
industries.note: The bill imposes new civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation, lets workers sue with multiplied damages, bans permanent replacement of strikers, and forces binding arbitration of first contracts. Employers that retaliate against organizing would face real financial consequences for the first time.

The bill removes obstacles to organizing — employer standing in elections, delay tactics, mandatory campaign meetings — lets unions and employers agree to fair-share fees over state right-to-work laws, and repeals bans on secondary boycotts. Union density and membership would likely grow.

Contractors must disclose three years of labor law violations, update them every six months, and risk losing awards or being referred for suspension and debarment; they must also provide paycheck transparency. Clean employers face mostly reporting burden, while violators risk losing federal business.

The bill adopts a worker-friendly test for who counts as an employee under the NLRA, narrowing which workers can be classified out of union protections. Gig-economy and staffing models that rely on contractor status would be harder to maintain.
